doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How Charlie Parker hit him and learning from McShann records
summary: Parker's sound and drive changed everything; he slowed down worn McShann records to learn phrases.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I’ve asked a few people from your generation how they felt and what the experience was like when they listened to Charlie Parker for the first time. You’ve told me that you heard “The Jumpin’ Blues” by Jay McShann...
Yeah, “Jumpin’ the Blues.”
...and you saw Bird in Chicago...it had to be 1944, because that’s when he was with Eckstine. Can you describe for me the impact he had on you at the time?

Well, he was different. He was just different. The sound was different. The way he played was different, the way he would drive when he played, the power behind his phrases. Just different. And everything was swinging. Just different from anybody else. You actually would have to live back during that era to understand it. Nobody else was playing that way, but him.
So it made you want to find out what he was doing...
Find out what he was doing and play the same way. Play it the same way, if possible.
How did you measure yourself in that regard? Did you just listen to the records over and over and over, and wear them out until you...

That’s what I did. Listened to the record. I’d wind the record down to the aluminum base. They had an aluminum base. I’d cut it down. And when I couldn’t get the phrases, I’d put it down to 33-1/3 speed. It would be in another key, but you could still get the phrases. If you cut it down, he sounded like Lester Young—if you cut down the speed.
How did you get the records?
I got them from the guys in Chicago. See, some guys in my band came from Chicago, and they brought the records out to the base, and they’d be playing them?
Which records at the time? The Guild records with Dizzy Gillespie and Sid Catlett?
Oh, no-no.
“Red Cross”? Or before that.
No. Way before that. Wasn’t nothing like that out.
Well, he made those dates in 1945, but I don’t know if they were out at the time.
No, I didn’t hear that until later.
But apart from “Jumpin’ Blues,” what other Charlie Parker solos did you learn...
“Jumpin’ the Blues” and “Sepian Bounce” with McShann. A couple of more tunes. But all of them were with McShann.
Everything with McShann. So your experience with Charlie Parker...
Was with McShann.
